body:
Have you checked with sanitizers to know for sure? This should be an easy leak to detect. 

We have documentation on using a variety of sanitizers https://docs.godotengine.org/en/latest/contributing/development/debugging/using_sanitizers.html#doc-using-sanitizers

If `old_capacity == 0` that implies zero memory is allocated for existing elements and hashes. The subsequent for loop then initializes the newly allocated memory, which is needed because the method's purpose is ensuring a target capacity and moving over any existing elements. AFAIK no data is destroyed and no allocations are leaked because in that condition there was no data to start with. That said, I don't know when `hash_table_size_primes[capacity_index] == 0` would be true anyways: https://github.com/godotengine/godot/blob/9d3b8792197b4cc8abb8f32bec37313b78233010/core/templates/hashfuncs.h#L534-L539

And for new hash maps where we would have minimum capacity but null element/hash pointers we have this lazy allocation before one of the two callsites for `_resize_and_rehash`:
https://github.com/godotengine/godot/blob/61accf060515416da07d913580419fd8c8490f7b/core/templates/hash_map.h#L200-L210

I think this code could definitely be improved (de-duplicate allocation/initialization code, remove unnecessary return path, make sure `EMPTY_HASH` is used when appropriate) but I don't think there's a leak/corruption issue

There is no memory leak here because: 
- It is a private method.
- This condition is never met, because old_capacity is never 0.
- Even if this condition were fulfilled, `old_elements` would not be allocated, because the old capacity is 0 (not the number of elements, but actually the size that is allocated).
- The sanitizers would easily catch it during unit tests.

> I think this code could definitely be improved (de-duplicate allocation/initialization code, remove unnecessary return path, make sure EMPTY_HASH is used when appropriate) but I don't think there's a leak/corruption issue

@a-johnston it's done here #90082.

So, I think this issue can be closed.

It was probably just left in from some prior implementation which allowed for allocating 0 capacity without that lazy init/allocation also happening. I can imagine someone keeping it in for safety without taking the time to realize it was a dead path. In any case, even if the first value of the allocation size list was 0 and it was possible, it wouldn't cause an issue. If this were allowed though your code has a bug where if `old_capacity == 0` we wouldn't allocate the new requested capacity.

If you read the git blame, this code was introduced when the HashMap implementation was updated in 2022. It wasn't there beforehand. Which is why I referenced the commit when the _first time this code was introduced_ in the original message.

Plus, there is no instance where this function would be called where it would matter if it should be resized if ``old_capacity`` is 0. That block is specifically there to _prevent_ resizing the values of that's true, because if ``old_capacity == 0``, there's something **_Seriously Wrong_**. All my patch does is tries to prevent any more corruption to data if SHTF. 

99.9999% of the time it'll do exactly what it does now, which resizes the HashMap. That 0.0001% where everything is on fire, it'll prematurely return without allocating anything, protecting the data and hashes, even though it probably doesn't matter if they are saved or not because the program is probably going to crash in the near future anyways.
This must allocate memory and if once old_capacity == 0, then elements and hashes were not allocated before.

@Nazarwadim
> This must allocate memory and if once old_capacity == 0, then elements and hashes were not allocated before.

But ``old_capacity`` _cannot be 0 **unless things are broken**_.

Let's look at where ``_resize_and_rehash()`` function is called:

The first time it's called is [Line 222](https://github.com/godotengine/godot/blob/08f9cba0fbf27f171dea55de6f8274928b9f0d84/core/templates/hash_map.h#L222), in the ``_insert()`` function.

The **first thing** the ``_insert()`` function does is get's the current capacity of the HashMap **and then makes sure memory has been allocated by checking if ``elements == nullptr``**. If that is true, it sets up the ``elements`` and ``hashes`` variables and allocates memory, and skips it otherwise. It then checks if the key already exists, and if it does, replaces the value, and if it doesn't, then checks to make sure the HashMap is big enough to take the new value, and if it isn't, calls ``_resize_and_rehash()``.

### _**So this first call to**_ ``_resize_and_rehash()`` _**already has elements and hashes allocated beforehand, and my patch would only protect that data if SHTF**_.

The second time it's called is [Line 451](https://github.com/godotengine/godot/blob/08f9cba0fbf27f171dea55de6f8274928b9f0d84/core/templates/hash_map.h#L451), in the ``reserve()`` function.

It firstly gets a capacity that will fit the amount requested by ``p_new_capacity``. If the current ``capacity_index`` and the local ``new_index`` are the same, it returns, not reaching the call to ``_resize_and_rehash()``. It then checks if the ``element`` variable is a nullptr, and if it is, **sets the ``capacity_index`` to the local ``new_index`` and returns _because nothing was allocated_**.

### _**So the second call to**_ ``_resize_and_rehash()`` _**already has elements and hashes allocated beforehand, and my patch would only protect that data if SHTF**_.

So no, ``_resize_and_rehash()`` does, in fact, **NOT** need to allocate memory **for the first time**. It **DOES** need to allocate memory **for a resize**.

I can spell things out a bit more simpler if you need, though I think I did a pretty good job at it so far.

Can you explain more specifically you mean by when things are broken/SHTF? Have you encountered a situation where this has happened or are you extrapolating from a cursory review of the code? The only thing I can think of off the top of my head is if you have a recast and mutation of `hash_table_size_primes` in between the initial allocation and then some subsequent call to `_resize_and_rehash` but even then with optimization flags the mutation would be omitted from the produced code due to it being `constexpr`. Either that or a full on hardware failure. But if we're entertaining either option, we can extend the exact same vague argument to not knowing if SHTF also has affected `capacity` or `hashes`, or even the code itself. In any case, this is not what typically is meant by memory leak/corruption.

> If you read the git blame, this code was introduced when the HashMap implementation was updated in 2022. It wasn't there beforehand. Which is why I referenced the commit when the first time this code was introduced in the original message.

It's a flattened commit although unfortunately at this point the original commits from the pr are no longer available. The prior implementation had a very similar "problem" which could lead to elements being freed without being copied to the new table if certain fields were mutated.

> Can you explain more specifically you mean by when things are broken/SHTF? Have you encountered a situation where this has happened or are you extrapolating from a cursory review of the code? The only thing I can think of off the top of my head is if you have a recast and mutation of `hash_table_size_primes` in between the initial allocation and then some subsequent call to `_resize_and_rehash` but even then with optimization flags the mutation would be omitted from the produced code due to it being `constexpr`. Either that or a full on hardware failure. But if we're entertaining either option, we can extend the exact same vague argument to not knowing if SHTF also has affected `capacity` or `hashes`, or even the code itself. In any case, this is not what typically is meant by memory leak/corruption.

The memory leak is in regards of if and when ``old_capacity == 0``. Based on the logic in the function, ``old_elements\old_hashes`` and ``elements\hashes`` become two different things when ``_resize_and_rehash()`` allocates more size to ``elements\hashes``, and doesn't free ``old_elements/old_hashes`` when returning if ``old_capacity == 0``. Even though now I know that _cannot_ happen in any sane way, and that check shouldn't exist.

The data corruption is in that same part of the code. _If_ ``old_elements\old_hashes`` _had data_, they were never reset as the class variables (``elements\hashes``), since those got reallocated before the function returned at the ``old_capacity == 0`` check. It's more data _loss_ than _corruption_, but I digress.

I saw what looked like an oversight of a possible memory leak, had the realization that it could corrupt/lose the memory it was holding, made this issue, then through the bickering learned that things were just kinda forgotten about throughout the years and what I was worried about only really matters if something happens in a very specific way.

The only reason why I was reading through the code was to learn and study it, and with my time working on microcontroller code for my Proxmark, I got really keen on things that look like they could be memory leaks (implementing a new memory manager will do that to a person, speaking of which I gotta get back to that). This, logically and by sight, fit those triggers, so I raised a fuss before actually going full bore into everything that it uses to work.

#90082 would technically fix this since it overhauls and improves these classes and functions, and it cleans up some dead code (of which the ``old_capacity == 0`` check is). Hell, passing the new resized capacity (and maybe the current capacity) into ``_resize_and_rehash()`` would work instead of needing ``_resize_and_hash()`` to redo the math both ``_insert()`` and ``reserve()`` already did to generate the current capacity of the hashmap (even though it's probably not a drop of water in the ocean, but _you already have the value_ so why not **use it**).

I think everyone agrees the code in question is harder to reason about than it should be due to the duplicated allocation/initialization code and dead code/impossible branch. The significance of the "bickering" though is that the issue of a data corruption/leak would be elevated and its fix likely backported to affected versions. I don't want to dissuade you from looking through the code and flagging potential issues or improvements, but yeah in this specific case I think https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/90082 does address the issue.
